notes: Disabled child's care plan judicial review; statutory duties and irrationality analysis are detailed and outcome is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Disabled child's care plan quashed for ignoring foster family

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970

key_facts: CD, a 15-year-old with quadriplegic cerebral palsy and partial blindness, challenged Isle of Anglesey County Council's June 2004 care plan.
For about two years she had spent five nights a week with foster carers Mr and Mrs R as respite from her mother, who has chronic fatigue syndrome.
The council proposed four nights boarding at Gogarth School, no overnight stays with Mr and Mrs R, and extensive support at the mother's adapted home.
CD consistently wished to board at school for only two nights and to continue substantial contact with Mr and Mrs R, whom she regarded as a second family.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the lawfulness of a local authority care plan for a looked-after disabled child.
enrichment.outcome: Care plan declared unlawful and set aside; decision to de-register Mr and Mrs R as foster carers also set aside; local authority directed to make a new plan.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority care plan for a disabled looked-after child is unlawful if it fails to promote welfare under the Children Act 1989, disregards the child's clearly expressed wishes about accommodation, ignores the mother's need for genuine respite rather than support workers alone, and abruptly ends an established foster placement without rational justification.
legal_issues: Whether the care plan unlawfully failed to discharge duties under sections 17, 20 and 23 of the Children Act 1989
Whether requiring four nights' boarding contrary to the child's wishes breached section 20(6)
Whether ending overnight placement with long-standing foster carers was irrational
Whether de-registration of foster carers linked to the unlawful plan was itself unlawful
linked_authorities: R v Gloucestershire County Council ex p Barry [1997] AC 584

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment with clear findings on each statutory duty and the care plan's unlawfulness.

notes: Attorney General unduly lenient sentence reference; starting point and mitigation analysis are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: two-year sentence for axe wounding not increased
key_facts: The offender bought a felling axe after provocation from two drunken men on a train and struck Nicholas Wright in the face.
The blow caused a severe facial injury and permanent impairment of movement on the right side of the victim's face.
He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment for wounding with intent after a late guilty plea.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient, arguing a five-year starting point after trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference on the ground that a sentence for wounding with intent was unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted but application refused; the two-year sentence was upheld as merciful but not unduly lenient.
enrichment.ratio: Where the starting point for wounding with intent after trial would be about five years, a judge may properly take a merciful course for a young man of previous good character, low reoffending risk, late guilty plea, and significant provocation, and the Court of Appeal will not interfere merely because the sentence is lenient.
legal_issues: Whether a two-year sentence for premeditated axe wounding with intent was unduly lenient
Appropriate starting point for wounding with intent after a not guilty plea
Weight to be given to good character, provocation, and late guilty plea
linked_authorities: Attorney General Reference No 24 of 1992 (1994) 15 Cr.App.R (S) 227
Attorney General Reference No 25 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr.App.R (S) 28
Attorney General Reference No 68 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr.App.R (S) 94

confidence.notes: Short judgment with explicit starting point, mitigating factors, and refusal to interfere.

notes: IHT tenant-in-common valuation appeal; jurisdiction and Lands Tribunal remittal issues are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: IHT half-share valuation remitted to Lands Tribunal

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Bernard Williams and his wife held Ash Lane Farm as tenants in common in equal shares; he died in February 2001.
A deed of variation vested his half share directly in his daughters, requiring valuation for inheritance tax.
The agreed vacant possession value was £550,000; the Revenue determined the deceased's share at a mathematical one-half.
The personal representatives contended the deceased's half was worth less because of the surviving spouse's occupation rights and related property effects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law under section 225 IHTA against preliminary decisions of the Special Commissioner.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; valuation issues remitted to the Lands Tribunal, which was not bound by the Commissioner's factual valuation conclusions.
enrichment.ratio: Whether section 161(4) related property provisions fixed a mathematical half-share was a question of law for the Special Commissioner, but the open market value of each tenant-in-common share and the impact of TOLATA occupation rights and section 171 death-related changes were valuation questions for the Lands Tribunal, not for the Commissioner to decide as fact.
legal_issues: Whether the Special Commissioner had jurisdiction or should have struck out the appeal as a land valuation matter
Whether section 161(4) required a mathematical half of vacant possession value
Whether TOLATA occupation rights and section 171 changes affected valuation
Whether the Commissioner erred by determining valuation facts herself
linked_authorities: Lynall v Inland Revenue Commissioners [1972] AC 680

confidence.notes: Revenue conceded several points; remaining issues on jurisdictional split and remittal are explicit.

notes: Forged co-owner mortgage and TOLATA postponed sale; equitable charge and section 14/15 analysis are well established.

enrichment.short_title: Forged mortgage binds husband's half-share; sale postponed five years

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Mrs Edwards lived with her children in a jointly owned house after divorce from her husband, who had disappeared.
The husband forged his wife's signature on a second mortgage deed to secure a £15,000 bank guarantee for his failed company.
Although the deed did not bind Mrs Edwards, the bank held an equitable charge over the husband's 50% beneficial interest.
The bank counterclaimed for sale under TOLATA; the house was worth about £200,000 with £60,000 owed to a prior lender.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim to remove a Land Registry caution and counterclaim for an order for sale of co-owned matrimonial home.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; bank's equitable charge over half the beneficial interest upheld; order for postponed sale after five years with review provisions.
enrichment.ratio: A mortgage deed with a forged co-owner signature is ineffective against the innocent owner but may create an equitable charge over the signing owner's beneficial interest under section 63 LPA 1925; on a TOLATA application the court must balance creditors' interests and children's welfare and may postpone sale where immediate sale would leave the occupying owner unable to rehouse.
legal_issues: Whether a forged mortgage deed created any security over the husband's beneficial half-share
Whether divorce transfer of the husband's interest to the wife was subject to the bank's charge
Whether the bank could obtain an order for sale of the entire property under TOLATA
What weight to give children's welfare and the occupying owner's financial hardship
linked_authorities: First National Securities Ltd v Hegerty [1985] QB 850
First National Bank plc v Achampong [2003] EWCA Civ 487
The Mortgage Corporation v Shaire [2000] 1 WLR 973
Bank of Ireland Home Mortgages Ltd v Bell [2001] 2 FLR 809
Penn v Bristol and West Building Society [1995] 2 FLR 938

confidence.notes: Well-established equitable charge principles applied; TOLATA outcome and five-year postponement clearly stated.

notes: Planning judicial review by litigant in person; inspector's reasoning upheld on open countryside and sustainability grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal dismissed: over-55s scheme in open countryside
key_facts: Mr Stanford appealed against an inspector's refusal of outline planning permission for over-55s accommodation at Graftonbury Garden Hotel, Hereford.
The inspector found the site was in open countryside, not a listed small settlement, and unsustainable for residential development.
The proposal would harm character and appearance, particularly woodland setting and trees on previously developed hotel land.
The claimant appeared in person and sought merits review rather than identification of legal error.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; inspector's decision held lawful; claimant ordered to pay £5,400 costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: A section 288 challenge succeeds only on error of law or irrationality, not because the court would have reached a different planning conclusion; qualitative judgments on open countryside status, sustainability, need, and visual impact are for the inspector unless no reasonable inspector could have reached the decision.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in treating Grafton as open countryside rather than a small settlement
Whether harm to trees and woodland setting rendered the development unacceptable
Whether the site was in a sustainable location for housing
Whether the inspector's general remarks precluded any future development beyond the hotel footprint

confidence.notes: Standard planning JR principles applied comprehensively; many claimant points were merits-based and rejected.

notes: Procedural ruling on Part 24 versus jurisdiction challenge; Rix authority in ECT Finance applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Summary judgment deferred pending jurisdiction challenge
key_facts: In Formula One-related litigation, defendants Bambino Holdings and the Argands challenged the court's jurisdiction.
The claimants also applied for summary judgment under CPR Part 24.
The applications were listed together by consent, but defendants contended jurisdiction must be decided first.
The court considered whether a claimant could pursue summary judgment while a Part 11 challenge remained outstanding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling on whether a Part 24 summary judgment application should be heard concurrently with Part 11 jurisdiction challenges.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment application not to be heard with the jurisdiction challenges; jurisdictional issues to be determined first.
enrichment.ratio: Although CPR Part 24 permits summary judgment with court permission before defence, a defendant who disputes jurisdiction should not ordinarily be drawn into merits evidence before that challenge is decided; the price of invoking English jurisdiction against foreign defendants is that they retain a real opportunity to decide whether to submit after an unsuccessful challenge.
legal_issues: Whether Part 24 summary judgment can be heard before determination of a Part 11 jurisdiction challenge
Effect of filing an acknowledgment of service while disputing jurisdiction
Whether the court should grant permission to proceed with summary judgment concurrently
linked_authorities: European Capital Trade Finance Ltd v Antenna Hungaria RT (27 March 1995)

confidence.notes: Procedural ruling only; merits of the underlying claim are not decided. Judgment text identifies Lewison J as the judge.

notes: Prison recategorisation judicial review for timeshare fraudster; flawed risk assessment reasons clearly quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Prison recategorisation quashed over compensation-order fears
key_facts: John Palmer was serving eight years for Tenerife timeshare conspiracy to defraud with a £2m compensation order and prior confiscation proceedings.
He was downgraded to category D for open conditions in November 2003 but recategorised back to C and then B before transfer to Springhill.
Governor Honey relied on outstanding compensation, possible £80m civil claims, press interest, and a gardens job near the perimeter.
By January 2004 the compensation order was fully secured and civil claims totalled about £4m with assets frozen.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of prison recategorisation decisions preventing transfer to open conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Recategorisation decisions declared flawed and set aside; fresh categorisation directed with opportunity for representations in exceptional circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: Prison categorisation must be based on escape risk and risk to the public if escape occurs, not on speculative civil litigation, media attention, or mischaracterised compensation obligations; decisions based on exaggerated financial exposure and irrelevant factors are unlawful and must be reconsidered.
legal_issues: Whether compensation and civil claim fears justified refusing open conditions
Whether categorisation criteria in Prison Service Order 0900 were properly applied
Whether the prisoner was entitled to advance representations before recategorisation
Whether judicial review was appropriate where an internal appeal existed
index_terms: R v SSHD ex p Allen
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p Allen (10 March 2000)
Hirst v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWCA Civ 378

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of PSO criteria and flawed reasons; fresh decision left to prison authorities.

notes: Occasional licences after quashed special removal; Bow Street authority and abuse of process arguments clearly rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Occasional licences upheld after quashed special removal
key_facts: The Court of Appeal quashed Ultimate Leisure's special removal of a licence from Mims Bar to the Gresham Hotel, Newcastle.
Ultimate applied for three consecutive three-week occasional licences to keep trading pending a fresh special removal application.
Rival Rindberg, a former objector, challenged the grants as abuse of process and contrary to the licensing scheme.
Magistrates granted the licences after hearing argument; police did not object.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash occasional licences granted by magistrates after quashing of a special removal on-licence.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; magistrates lawfully granted consecutive occasional licences under section 180.
enrichment.ratio: Section 180 occasional licences may cover circumstances giving rise to a need to sell liquor at other premises, including the hiatus after a quashed licence pending a fresh application; applying for such licences was not an abuse of process or collateral attack on the Court of Appeal judgment, and magistrates did not usurp licensing justices by granting short-term cover while a opposed fresh application awaited determination.
legal_issues: Whether applying for occasional licences was an abuse of process after declining a stay
Whether section 180 permits licences pending a fresh special removal application
Whether consecutive occasional licences frustrated the statutory licensing scheme
Whether magistrates usurped the function of licensing justices
index_terms: Bow Street ex p Commissioner of Police
linked_authorities: R v Bow Street Stipendiary Magistrates, ex p Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [1983] 2 All ER 915
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Clear application of Bow Street principles; abuse of process and scheme arguments comprehensively rejected.

notes: Family contact appeal resolved by consent on Iranian mirror orders; mediation delay noted but outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Contact appeal allowed pending Iranian mirror orders
key_facts: Iranian-origin parents disputed contact arrangements for sons aged 12 and 8 after four-day Family Division proceedings before Hedley J.
The mother appealed against insufficient safeguards before unsupervised contact was extended.
Mediation ordered in February 2003 did not proceed until February 2004 and failed in April 2004.
During argument the parties agreed on Iranian divorce with Hezana/mirror orders and freedom-of-movement protections.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against contact order conditions, listed after delayed mediation following permission granted in February 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; unsupervised contact extension deferred until Iranian divorce incorporating mirror custody orders and mother's freedom-of-movement declaration.
enrichment.ratio: Where parents agree that children's welfare requires unsupervised contact but also Iranian mirror orders within a consensual divorce, the court should facilitate that solution rather than continue dispute over prior contact safeguards that events have overtaken.
legal_issues: Whether contact should move from supervised to unsupervised without Iranian mirror orders
Whether safeguards required mirror orders incorporated in an Iranian divorce
Whether the mother needed a freedom-of-movement declaration in Iran
Effect of protracted mediation on the appeal issues

confidence.notes: Consensual resolution reached in court; detailed merits of Hedley J's order not revisited.

notes: PlayStation mod-chip CDPA summary judgment application; s296 analysis is detailed with partial fact issues remaining.

enrichment.short_title: Sony mod-chip case: partial summary judgment on CDPA anti-circumvention
key_facts: Sony sued Mr Ball for importing and selling Messiah2 chips that circumvent PlayStation 2 copy-protection and regional coding.
The chips enable unauthorised game copies and foreign-region games to be played on modified consoles.
Playing a game copies program and artistic works into RAM for a fraction of a second during use.
Mr Ball argued RAM copies are not 'articles', export sales do not create UK infringing copies, and back-up or PAL-use purposes defeat liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 24 summary judgment application against one defendant in multi-party proceedings alleging breach of CDPA anti-copy-protection provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Partial resolution only: sales to UK customers and UK-targeted publications breach s296; export stock and some s296ZD issues require trial; back-up and hardware-only arguments rejected.
enrichment.ratio: A transient copy of copyright works in RAM is an 'infringing copy' under section 27 CDPA; section 296 requires knowledge that devices will be used to make infringing copies in the UK, so export-only stock may not breach until destination is known, but section 296ZD creates stricter liability for promoting devices to circumvent effective technological measures applied to copyright works.
legal_issues: Whether transient RAM copies are infringing 'articles' under section 27
Whether export of mod chips avoids section 296 knowledge requirement
Whether back-up copies or PAL-only home use authorise circumvention
Whether copy-protection on hardware rather than software falls within sections 296 and 296ZD

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis but summary judgment granted only in part; export-stock liability remains fact-sensitive.
